transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-23
Start time: 14:30 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Aisha (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Samir (BrightScale Lead ML Eng), Maya (Infra), Olivia (CTO)
Shared: throughput-bench spreadsheet (drive.google.com/bs-throughput), Redwood deck (https://redwood.ai/decks/throughput-bench.pdf)

[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro - i'm aisha, i'll run the commercial side but ethan will lead the deep tech portion. Samir, Maya, Olivia - thanks for making time.
[00:12] Samir: yeah thanks, we wanted this to be fairly technical. our primary ask: get predictable throughput at 2000 reqs/min for our chat endpoints with p95 latency under 350ms.
[00:20] Ethan: great, that's helpful. quick clarification: is that 2000 concurrent short-turn user requests or longer context sessions?
[00:28] Maya: majority are short, median seq ~60 tokens, tail up to 800 tokens about 5% of the time. so we care about p95 and p99 tail.
[00:36] Olivia: and we run in our VPC, prefer private deployment, but open to dedicated hosted if latency/cost better. security is required - SOC2 plus KMS.

[01:10] Ethan: ok good, i'll walk through how Redwood's runtime approaches continuous batching, scheduler knobs, and the important knobs like max_num_seqs, token caps, and kv cache behavior. then we can map to your traffic shape and pick a benchmark plan.
[01:28] Ethan: first, continuous batching - instead of fixed batch windows we operate a continuous enqueue. requests are grouped by compatible model variant and sequence length buckets. this means high burst tolerance and lower per-token cost, but you need to tune the scheduler to balance latency SLO against throughput.
[01:45] Maya: can you explain scheduler knobs? we've seen references to target_latency_ms, max_batch_size, and max_num_seqs - not sure how they interplay.
[01:55] Ethan: yeah. short version: target_latency_ms tells the scheduler how long to hold a batch before sending. max_batch_size caps GPU batch dimensions; max_num_seqs caps number of sequences in a batch for multi-seq packing. so if you have many short sequences, increasing max_num_seqs raises utilization but can bump p95 if target_latency_ms is high.
[02:20] Samir: we've tried bumping max_batch_size but saw p95 worsen; suspect KV cache thrashing?
[02:28] Ethan: good point. for chat applications KV cache (we sometimes see it transcribed as KV "cash" in notes) grows with seq length and with concurrent sessions since every active session keeps an entry. high max_num_seqs increases parallel sequences and the cumulative KV memory, which can force kernel choices that are less optimal or cause more memory copies. that's a common root cause of throughput regressions.

[03:15] Ethan: practical tuning order we recommend: first, profile seq length distribution; second, set max_num_seqs roughly to median_short_burst * (GPU_util_target / single_seq_util); third, cap per-request token limit to reduce worst-case KV pressure; fourth, enable prefix/KV caching for repeated prefixes and sticky routing for long-lived sessions.
[03:45] Maya: when you say cap per-request token limit, do you mean on the Redwood side or application-level?
[03:52] Ethan: we mean set a practical limit in your request path - e.g., reject or truncate requests over 1024 tokens at the API layer - and then let the runtime enforce max_tokens_per_request too. This reduces KV cache growth and keeps kernel selection in the low-latency path.

[04:30] Samir: example numbers? our current config is max_num_seqs=8, max_batch_size=256, target_latency_ms=120. throughput is ~1.2k rps with p95 ~420ms which fails our goal.
[04:45] Ethan: ok quick mental model: with median 60 tokens and tail 800, max_num_seqs=8 is conservative. If you bump max_num_seqs to 12 or 16 and lower target_latency_ms to 80ms, continuous batching will fill larger multi-seq packs more aggressively, raising throughput but you risk some queuing latency. However p95 likely goes down if we avoid kernel thrash - because a bigger packed kernel is more efficient. The key is to also cap token limits and use kv caching to reduce repeated prefix cost.

[06:00] Olivia: what about quantization? we want int8 to reduce memory and increase throughput, but worried about accuracy regression.
[06:10] Ethan: quantization (int8/4-bit) often gives big throughput wins - smaller KV footprint, faster matmuls - but you need evals against your prompt set. Redwood Optimize suggests model+quant profiles: for many open models int8 gives ~1.6-2x throughput. we can provide quantized variants in dedicated pools. downside: small accuracy delta especially on instruction-following or safety-critical ops - we'd recommend an eval job on your top 1000 prompts.
[06:38] Samir: can you run a quick benchmark with int8 vs fp16 and report p95/p99?
[06:42] Ethan: yes - action item. we'll run with the same workload: max_num_seqs=16, token cap 1024, two concurrency profiles (2x and 4x baseline). link to spreadsheet once done.

[07:20] Ethan: another important detail is scheduler preemption and priority routing. Redwood supports soft priority tokens so you can prefer low-latency traffic (e.g., interactive chat) while letting background jobs be batched more aggressively onto cheaper capacity. For VPC/on-prem this is configurable via the control plane to ensure tenant isolation.

[08:05] Maya: on VPC, any differences in kernel selection or batching strategy? we've seen differences when we moved from hosted to on-prem GPUs.
[08:15] Ethan: kernel selection is hardware-aware; on-prem may have different GPU families (A100 vs H100 vs L40). That affects convolution/matmul kernels and memory behavior. The runtime probes at startup and picks optimized kernels. The batching strategy is the same but you may need to adjust max_batch_size to match the GPU memory and how many sequences fit in KV cache. we usually run a short hardware sweep to pick defaults.

[09:00] Samir: about KV cache eviction - if many sessions are idle, do you evict older KV entries?
[09:08] Ethan: yes, we have an LRU-like policy and tunable eviction thresholds. but eviction costs you reloads if sessions resume. that's where sticky routing and session-affinity to a worker helps: keep active sessions on the same worker to reuse KV in-GPU memory. In Dedicated pools we can reserve a portion of GPU memory for long-lived KV to avoid thrash.

[10:30] [transcription artifact: speaker overlap, small crosstalk]
[10:35] Samir: is there a hard limit on number of sessions per GPU?
[10:38] Ethan: no single hard limit - it's practical limits based on KV memory and compute for your model. We give guidance: for a 70B model with fp16 you might fit ~3000 short sessions per A100 with aggressive packing; with int8 that number increases. but these are workload-specific, hence the benchmarks.

[12:00] Ethan: demo plan for benchmarks: 1) baseline test with your current config (max_num_seqs=8, target_latency_ms=120), 2) run config A: max_num_seqs=12, target_latency_ms=80, token_cap=1024, 3) run config B: max_num_seqs=16, token_cap=1024, quant=int8, 4) run priority-mix test with 80/20 interactive/background. We'll capture p50/p95/p99, throughput, GPU util, and KV memory.
[12:40] Maya: how long will each test run? we need stable tails so at least 10 minutes steady-state?
[12:45] Ethan: recommend 15 minutes per config to capture p99 tails and ramp behavior. total run about 60 minutes per full sweep - matches availability.

[13:30] Olivia: regarding security - you mentioned KMS and audit logs earlier. how do we get those in VPC/private?
[13:38] Aisha: on the commercial side, Redwood Private offers KMS integration and audit logs shipped to your SIEM. we'll attach SOC2 and ISO attestation in the follow-up. action: share security docs.

[14:10] Samir: quick question on batching heuristics: is there a way to prefer multi-seq packing only when latency headroom exists? we don't want packing to increase tail latency for some VIP users.
[14:20] Ethan: yes - scheduler supports conditional packing thresholds: you can set a per-route latency SLO and the scheduler will only pack beyond X if estimated latency impact < Y. this is an approximation but works well. You can also mark routes as low-latency and they get priority slots.

[15:05] [00:15:05 - Ethan shares a short screen with the runtime dashboard, some metrics readouts referenced: p95 380ms -> 220ms after packing adjustments; kv memory plots show step-change]

[17:00] Samir: the kv memory plot - we see spikes coincident with long requests, is there a mitigation?
[17:08] Ethan: two mitigations: token capping to avoid huge KV growth, and session-affinity plus reserving KV pages for high-priority sessions. also consider chunked generation for extremely long contexts.

[18:30] Maya: will enabling quantization change KV format? there's an interplay there?
[18:36] Ethan: yes quantization can change KV storage size; int8 reduces KV footprint, which reduces memory pressure and can prefer faster kernels. but conversion overhead during model load is small. we surface quant profiles in the model catalog so you know per-model impacts.

[20:00] Olivia: any gotchas for on-prem networking? e.g., MTU, driver versions?
[20:08] Ethan: yes, ensure latest CUDA/CUDF drivers we recommend, and check RDMA configs for multi-node batching (if you plan cross-node batching). MTU tuning and NIC drivers help. We'll include a VPC/on-prem checklist.

[22:10] [small side discussion about pricing: Aisha describes Dedicated vs Private pricing, not fully transcribed here]

[25:00] Samir: last piece - we'd like a simple recommended config to try first in our staging env.
[25:08] Ethan: recommended starter: max_num_seqs=12, max_batch_size=320 (depends on GPU), target_latency_ms=80, token_cap=1024, enable prefix KV caching, sticky routing for chat sessions, quantize candidate models to int8 for a second run. Run the benchmark A/B and share results.

[26:40] Samir: great. if results show p95 under 350ms at 2k RPM, what are next steps for Dedicated?
[26:48] Aisha: we'll propose Dedicated capacity sizing and estimated cost per 1M tokens; if you want Private on-prem, engineering will scope the VPC deployment and service contract.

[28:00] Ethan: to wrap - i'll run the bench with the configs we discussed. we'll capture GPU util, queue depth, KV memory, p50/95/99 and attach the raw log. we'll also test int8 vs fp16.

[28:25] Maya: for the benchmark, how do we simulate your sticky routing? can we share a session key distribution?
[28:35] Ethan: yes send a sample of session ids and seq length distribution; if you can't share raw data we'll accept histograms. ideal: per-request sequence length histogram and concurrency pattern over 24 hours.

[30:00] [brief pause, crosstalk]
[30:10] Samir: ok i'll pull that histogram and share by EOD tomorrow.
[30:15] Aisha: i'll share SOC2 and VPC checklist by Tuesday.

[30:40] Olivia: one last question: in your experience what's the biggest single config change that improves throughput for chat workloads?
[30:48] Ethan: usually it's increasing max_num_seqs with careful token caps plus moving to int8. Those two together often give the biggest step function improvement. Second is sticky routing to avoid KV thrash.

[31:30] [closing recap - next steps read out]
[31:40] Aisha: recap: Ethan runs benchmarks (configs A/B), send result spreadsheet link; Aisha sends security docs and pricing; Samir shares histograms; follow-up meeting scheduled for 2026-09-02.
[31:58] Samir: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[32:05] Olivia: thanks - appreciate the details.
[32:10] Ethan: thanks all.

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcription occasionally mislabels technical tokens (KV cache -> KV cash, max_num_seq vs max_num_seqs), and there is mild crosstalk during screen share.
